questions.question: On the periodic table, iron is written Fe, gold Au, silver Ag and lead Pb. None of these symbols matches the element's English name. Where do their letters come from?
choices: The elements' names in Latin
The elements' names in Greek
The names of the people who found them
The names of the places they were found
questions.context: Many symbols come straight from an element's name, such as H for hydrogen and O for oxygen, but these four come from Latin: ferrum for iron, aurum for gold, argentum for silver and plumbum for lead, the root of the word plumbing. The symbols were built from Latin names so that the same letters stand for each element in every language. Einsteinium, named after Albert Einstein, and americium, named after the Americas, have symbols that follow their English names: Es and Am.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade periodic table lessons teach that each element has a one- or two-letter symbol, and that some, such as Fe and Au, come from Latin names.

questions.question: A goldbeater pounds a small square of gold again and again until it spreads into a leaf so thin that light shines through it. What property of metals lets the gold spread so far without cracking?
choices: Malleability
Ductility
Lustre
Conductivity
questions.context: A malleable metal can be hammered or pressed into thin sheets without cracking, and gold is the most malleable metal of all: a single gram can be beaten into a sheet of about one square metre. Ductility is the related property of being drawn out into wire, lustre is a metal's shine, and conductivity is how well it carries heat and electricity.
questions.grade_note: Shiny, malleable, ductile and good conductors are the metal properties a 6th grader learns, and telling malleable (sheets) from ductile (wire) is the usual mix-up.

questions.question: A student shades every metal on a chart of the periodic table, leaving the other elements blank. Which part of the chart ends up shaded?
questions.answer: Most of it, from the left across the middle
choices: Most of it, from the left across the middle
About half of it, all down the left side
About a third of it, across the middle
A small part of it, in the top right corner
questions.context: About four in five elements are metals: they fill the left side and the middle of the table, and the two rows printed below it as well. The nonmetals gather in the top right corner, apart from hydrogen at the top left, and the metalloids sit along the staircase line between the two.
questions.grade_note: That most elements are metals, on the left and in the middle of the table, is the first sorting rule a 6th grader learns for the periodic table.

questions.question: Germanium is a metalloid with a grey metallic shine. A chemist sets a small lump of it on a steel block and strikes it hard with a hammer. What happens to the lump?
choices: It shatters into small pieces
It flattens into a thin sheet
It bends but does not break
It dents but holds together
questions.context: Metalloids usually look like metals but behave largely like nonmetals. Germanium is crystalline and brittle, so a hard blow breaks it apart, where the same blow would only flatten a lump of gold or lead. Silicon, the best-known metalloid, has a metallic shine too, and it is brittle as well.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade lessons teach that metalloids have some properties of each kind: a metal's shine, but a nonmetal's brittleness.

questions.question: Carbon and sulfur are nonmetals that are solid at room temperature, and bromine is one that is liquid. Oxygen and neon are nonmetals too, and each is a gas. What are the seventeen nonmetals like at room temperature?
choices: Most of them are gases
Most of them are liquids
Most of them are brittle solids
Most of them are shiny, bendable solids
questions.context: Eleven of the seventeen nonmetals are gases at room temperature: hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, chlorine and the six noble gases, such as helium and neon. The other six are five brittle solids, among them carbon, sulfur and iodine, and bromine, the one liquid; shiny, bendable solids are metals. Every element that is a gas at room temperature is a nonmetal, since all metals but mercury are solid, and so are the metalloids.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade lessons teach that nonmetals sit apart from metals in their states as well as their looks: many are gases at room temperature, where every metal but mercury is a solid.

questions.question: A pale yellow element has no metallic shine. It crumbles when struck with a hammer, and almost no electricity passes through it. Where on the periodic table does it sit?
choices: On the right side
On the left side
Across the middle
Along the staircase line
questions.context: Those are a nonmetal's properties, and the element is sulfur, which sits with most of the nonmetals on the right side of the table. Solid nonmetals are brittle and carry heat and electricity poorly, while the metals on the left and in the middle bend, flatten and conduct. The metalloids along the staircase line between them are brittle too, but they shine like metals.
questions.grade_note: Sorting an element as a metal, nonmetal or metalloid from its properties, and finding where it sits on the table, is the core skill of the 6th-grade standard (TEKS 6.6C).

questions.question: The chips inside computers and phones are built on thin slices of silicon, a metalloid. What makes silicon the right material for them?
questions.answer: It can be made to carry electricity or block it
choices: It can be made to carry electricity or block it
It lets electricity through more easily than copper
It blocks all electricity, just the way glass does
It is magnetic, the way iron and steel are
questions.context: Silicon is a semiconductor: it carries electricity far less easily than a metal such as copper, but far more easily than glass, and adding tiny amounts of other elements changes how much it carries. A computer's processor chip holds billions of tiny silicon switches, called transistors, that turn the flow of electricity on and off. Silicon is not magnetic, and like other metalloids it is brittle.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade lessons give silicon as the example metalloid and teach that its in-between conducting is why it is used in computer chips.

cb5af24cff.why: Judge (low, tell): 'hammers' sat next to the answer's root (malle-, as in mallet). The stem now says 'pounds', which loosens the link. Same fact (F11, F13); key, choices and context unchanged.

83a2e7610d.why: Judge (low, tell): 'About half of it, all down the right side' was the weakest lure; few students put the metals on the right. It is now 'About a third of it, across the middle', the belief that only the middle block is metal; metals are about four in five (F7). Stem, key and context unchanged.

e0dc450516.why: Judge (high, tell; medium, grade): 'every gas element is a nonmetal' was answerable by common sense (nobody takes oxygen or helium for a metal). Re-keyed, as the judge proposed, to the scope's own line 'many are gases': most nonmetals are gases (11 of 17, F14). The stem names two solids, a liquid and two gases, so no state is left over to guess; the lures are the brittle solids the unit teaches nonmetals to be (F16), the liquid bromine (F14) and the metals' picture (F11). The old fact moves to the context.

2755f26b12.why: Judge (medium, tell): 'It can be drawn out into long, thin wires' was nearly dead beside a stem about thin slices, and the key was the longest choice. That lure is now 'It is magnetic, the way iron and steel are' (the mix-up with magnetic disks; silicon is diamagnetic, F25, checked now), and the key is shortened to 'It can be made to carry electricity or block it' (same fact, F21). Fact-check polish taken: 'A computer's processor chip holds billions'. Stem unchanged.

ee90d6cb70.why: Fact-check error: not every electric car motor holds neodymium (permanent-magnet motors are 84-86% of the market, F26), so the stem now says 'Most electric car motors' and 'the speakers in most headphones' (F27, checked now). Judge (medium, tell): two lures died on other facts ('A microchip' on this unit's silicon question). 'A microchip' is now 'A battery', the strong lure for an electric car; a battery is not part of a motor, a generator or a speaker. 'A wire coil' stays: all three devices really hold one, so knowing a speaker has a magnet no longer settles it. Key and context unchanged.

dropped.question: Most electric car motors, the generators in many wind turbines and the speakers in most headphones hold a part made with neodymium, one of the rare earth elements. What is that part?
dropped.why: failed the re-check: The judge's main tell is not fixed. The stem still names the three textbook magnet devices: motors, generators and speakers. NGSS MS-PS2-3, at this same grade band, gives motors and generators as its examples of devices that use magnetic force, so the answer comes without knowing neodymium. 'A wire coil' still dies on copper wire (electric-circuits keys copper wires), 'A switch' is weak, and 'A battery' fits neither a generator nor a speaker. The judge's fix for the stem was not taken. The facts check out: most EV motors are permanent-magnet (about 86-94%), and neodymium is the usual magnet in headphone drivers.
